palette: pale oak and warm white with fresh green
topic: asking for the one thing a preset cannot say
angle: Presets cover the look. They cannot cover the sentence in your head about your own room. The prompt bar takes that sentence verbatim, so the post prints the typed line as a pull quote and puts the render it produced directly underneath it. Input above, output below, nothing in between.
visualSummary: The pale wash ground, which nothing else in the recent grid uses. A large opening quote mark in brand pale, then a single typed instruction set as a big two line pull quote in the deep brand blue. Beneath it an attribution row naming the prompt bar rather than a person, no avatar. Below that a wide rounded photo card holding a scandinavian home office: a long oak worktop running the full width of a bright three panel window and fixed under it, a white column radiator beneath the worktop, a light wood chair centred in front with a knitted throw over its back, a monitor and keyboard on the worktop, two small potted plants on the sill at the left, a low open bookcase at the far left, a small drawer unit at the right, framed abstract prints on both side walls and a domed pendant hanging centrally, on a warm oak plank floor. The photograph carries no pill and no scrim, so it is shown undimmed. The footer carries the virtually staged line and a single call to action pill.

copy.headline: Put the desk under the window, not against the wall.
copy.caption:
That sentence is the whole prompt. One line typed into the box, and the room below is what came back.

Presets get you a look. They cannot tell the model anything about your room.

This room has one good window and a radiator sitting under it. Put the desk against a side wall and you have wasted the only decent light in the place. No preset has an opinion about that. A sentence does.

So here is what was typed, in full:

"Put the desk under the window, not against the wall."

That is the entire instruction. The Scandinavian preset did the rest: the oak, the white walls, the floor, the plants on the sill.

The room was empty when this started. No desk, no chair, no shelves, no lamp, nothing on the sill. Every object in the photo was generated from one photograph of an empty room and that one line of text.

You do not have to describe a whole room. You have to say the one thing you would tell a stager if you were paying for one.

What would yours say?

Try it on a photo of a room in your own house. Link in bio.

Virtually staged with Stagify.ai

data._imagePillNote: Deliberately absent. photoCard couples the pill to card__scrim, a bottom gradient reaching 82 per cent opacity, so adding a pill drove the lower half of the photograph dark: the oak floor read as grey brown and the room stopped looking like the pale oak and warm white the post claims for it. On a frame whose whole job is to show what the typed sentence produced, dimming the product to label it is the wrong trade. The attribution row above already says the quote is an input, so the photograph directly beneath it needs no second caption to be read as the output.

params.additionalPrompt: Put the desk under the window, not against the wall.

generation.modelNote: additionalPrompt is the post. It carries the free text a customer types into the prompt bar, and the card prints that same string as its quote, so the two must stay byte identical. No palette, composition or lighting direction was added alongside it: the Scandinavian preset is the rest of the request, exactly as it would be for a user. labelVirtuallyStaged is left off, as on every post except 08-19, because the template chrome already carries the disclosure line and a burnt in badge would say it twice. Rule 3 otherwise untouched: gemini-3.1-flash-image, full retry loop, never skipQualityReview.
generation.authorNote: Rule 4 was what saved this post, twice, and neither catch was an artifact. First pass: score 100, quality.perfect true, a clean render, and unusable. Its source had the window in the LEFT wall at a steep oblique angle, so the model put the desk near the window running out into the middle of the room. A defensible reading of the sentence, but nothing in the frame reads as under anything, and a post that invites the viewer to check the instruction against the picture cannot have a payoff that needs explaining. Fixed in the source screen, not the prompt: the window must now sit in the camera facing wall. Second pass found the right room and then failed on the other half. The prompt at that point ended "Keep the chair tucked under it", and across six attempts on three source photos the model never once tucked the chair, so the card would have printed an instruction the picture visibly half ignored. That clause was cut and the room restaged, rather than trimming the quote and keeping the render, which would have made the caption a lie about what was typed. A third pass then kept every candidate instead of the best by score, because score does not separate these outcomes: the previous best by score was an 80 whose chair had a four star swivel base AND two conventional rear legs, the account's documented artifact, while a clean chair also comes back 80. Four candidates were opened side by side and one chosen by eye. That first choice was still wrong, and the step 8 reviewer caught it: on candidate three the chair's front-left leg forks into two parallel members ending in flat chopped tips about eleven pixels apart in height, with no rounded foot and no contact shadow, so it stops in mid air while the other three plant cleanly. Confirmed at full zoom before acting on the report, because a reviewer naming the account's known artifact is exactly the claim most likely to be pattern matched rather than seen. Candidate four replaced it, from the same batch and the same prompt, so this was a choice between candidates rather than another generation. It is also the stronger frame on its own merits: the desk is a worktop fixed under the full width of the window, which states the instruction more plainly than a freestanding desk near it, and being wall mounted it has no legs at all, which removes half the artifact surface. Its chair carries four single tapered legs, each ending in a rounded foot with its own contact shadow, and a throw over the back covers the seat frame. The chair sits below the worktop line and small in the frame, so the element most likely to fail is the one the composition looks at last.

devilsAdvocate.whyThisOne: Every other surviving candidate asks the reader to believe an output. This one hands them an input. It is the first post to show the product taking an instruction in the user's own words, the prompt bar has never been posted, and it is the only candidate whose feature has a proof in the config catalog that the frame delivers literally rather than by implication: the one specific request a preset cannot express, and the result. It is also buildable with tooling that already exists, since free text reaches the model through additionalPrompt on the interior staging path, so the quoted sentence and the render underneath it are the same event.
devilsAdvocate.residualRisk: The inset has to prove the sentence, so the desk cannot be cropped out, and a desk under a window is backlit, which is precisely where the model's leg geometry fails. The known defect is extra or disconnected legs scoring 70 to 85, subtle at feed size and obvious at full size, and a small inset that a reader is checking against a quoted instruction is an invitation to open the image. There is no fallback composition: the crop that would hide a fifth leg is the crop that deletes the desk. It materialised exactly as predicted on the second staging round, and was answered by opening four candidates side by side rather than accepting a best attempt, not by cropping.
devilsAdvocate.evidenceCaveat: The ranking is a reasoned argument, not an evidenced one. history/metrics.jsonl does not exist and not one post on this account has ever been measured, so nothing here rests on past performance and the mechanism this post proposes is a hypothesis it should be used to test.
devilsAdvocate.userDirection: The user left format to the advocate rather than fixing it in advance, and approved i05 unchanged. The advocate chose single 4:5 over carousel and story: the mechanism is one sentence the reader finishes before deciding anything, so hiding the payoff behind a swipe taxes the exact beat that converts, a story leaves the grid in 24 hours when the first artifact proving the product takes instructions should be permanent, and a single needs one render rather than the three to five a carousel would put through a quality loop that fails on desk legs.

round1.blocking: Chair front-left leg carries the account's documented artifact: it forks into two parallel wood toned members running side by side for the last 60px of the 2x archive and terminating in two flat notched chops about 11px apart in height, with neither the rounded dowel foot, the contact shadow nor the board reflection the other three feet all have. Below the chop only a 2px dark hairline continues toward the floor, so the leg reads as ending in mid air. Subtle in the 400px thumb, visible in the bottom left quadrant of the 1080 upload at ordinary zoom.
round1.action: Verified at full zoom before acting, because a reviewer naming a known artifact is the claim most likely to be pattern matched rather than seen. It was real. Replaced with candidate four from the same batch and the same prompt, which is a choice between existing candidates rather than a new generation, and re-rendered.

round2.legAudit: Clean. Exactly four chair legs, each a single tapered dowel from frame to floor with no fork, no doubling, no break and no float, each ending in a rounded foot with its own dark contact ellipse. The four contact points form a coherent parallelogram on one floor plane: the far edge is correctly shorter than the near edge and the two rails are parallel to within 1px of slope. The worktop is wall hung and fully cantilevered with no leg to fail, the drawer unit sits on casters with a contact shadow, and the bookcase base meets the floor on an unbroken line.
round2.claimCheck: Supported without hesitation. The worktop runs the full width of the window wall directly beneath the opening and is centred on the window to within 0.9 per cent, the monitor sits mid window on it and the chair faces the glass, so the occupant's sightline is out of the window, which is the point of the instruction. Both alternative walls are visibly kept clear of any desk, so the viewer can see the declined option.
round2.dashAudit: No dash-like character anywhere in the frame, in the chrome or inside the photograph. Zero hyphens, zero en dashes, zero em dashes. The longest horizontal marks in the type are the t crossbars at roughly half the advance width of an adjacent lowercase n, and the decorative quote glyph is 1.45 times the height of an n on a vertical long axis, so neither is dash-like in orientation or aspect.

nitsNotFixed: Radiator plumbing. Both riser pipes stand on the floor correctly but their top ends stop dead at mid radiator height joined to nothing, and four small chrome valve blobs sit clear of the fins attached to nothing. It is the ends-in-mid-air family, on plumbing rather than furniture. Each element is 6 to 15px wide at 1080 and invisible in the thumbnail, and radiator valves plausibly read as small chrome lumps, so it survives at feed size. Left as a known nit rather than spending the third render the playbook's two round cap does not allow.

Disclosure contrast. 'Virtually staged with Stagify.ai' fails WCAG AA on the pale wash. Measured against the real token rather than a screen sample: _macros.js line 147 sets .disclosure--dark to rgba(31, 41, 55, .6), which over --brand-wash #eff6ff composites to rgb(114,123,135) for 3.94:1 against a 4.5:1 requirement at this weight and size. Alpha .68 would give 4.96:1. NOT changed here on purpose: this is shared chrome, quote-card is the only template that passes dark: true so this post is the first ever affected, and altering a shared design token is a design system decision rather than a post decision. Raised with the user instead.

Headline line one clears the right safe margin by 6px at 1080. Nothing is clipped and both the final t and the comma render complete, but there is no slack, and overflow is hidden so growth would fail silently.
The source photograph's own crop slices the right wall gallery cluster mid mat. Not a renderer overflow.
